name: Berlin
summary_text: Berlin is a Land of the Federal Republic of Germany. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that federal floor. Legal gender recognition is therefore governed nationally, not by the Berlin Senate.  The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force from 1 November 2024, replaced the 1980 Transsexuals Act, whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. Transgender, intersex and non-binary adults can change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, and it was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only.  Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage.  Berlin's own prison service states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that its staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it sets out gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin. How the exception is applied in practice is unsettled, and outcomes have gone both ways. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle said Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia, DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.  Recorded anti-LGBTI violence in Berlin is high by national standards. MANEO, the city's anti-violence documentation project, logged 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports — a new high for reporting volume. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and in streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten the most affected districts, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025.  At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, MANEO reports that a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled. The project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily 17:00 to 19:00.  Nationally the picture is one of rising pressure on Pride events. The amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events across Germany in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including an attack with boiling water, and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany. Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades such as Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police. Berlin CSD organisers have publicly urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of attendees expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.  Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024. According to her account, reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.  Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.  Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle said Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia, DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.  Recorded anti-LGBTI violence in Berlin is high by national standards. MANEO, the city's anti-violence documentation project, logged 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports — a new high for reporting volume. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and in streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten the most affected districts, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025.  At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, MANEO reports that a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled. The project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily 17:00 to 19:00.  Nationally the picture is one of rising pressure on Pride events. The amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events across Germany in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including an attack with boiling water, and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany. Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades such as Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police. Berlin CSD organisers have publicly urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of attendees expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.  Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024. According to her account, reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.  Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.  Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

name: England
summary_text: England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework. Passport and document rules, entry and visa rules, marriage law and criminal law are uniform across the country, and the single-sex-services regime operates through the national equality legislation and the national equality watchdog, with no devolved layer between a visitor and those institutions. The United Kingdom Supreme Court sits in London and the Equality and Human Rights Commission's headquarters are in England, so the machinery that governs a trans visitor's day here is the machinery of the whole state.  The defining judgment is the unanimous ruling of the United Kingdom Supreme Court in For Women Scotland, handed down on 16 April 2025. The court held that "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, and that a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge said the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. Those definitions govern services, searches and detention allocation in England.  The Equality and Human Rights Commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, updated its code of practice after the Supreme Court ruling. As reported on 20 May 2025, the code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for their birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor meets at venues, on transport and in services from day to day.  Prison and custody allocation follows the same principle. On 19 June 2026 Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down Scottish Prison Service guidance that had allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis in line with the April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment. A judicial review reported on 5 February 2026 tested how far the April 2025 ruling reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide: government lawyers argued that a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy "Orwellian".  The Home Office's England-and-Wales hate-crime statistics, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand fell 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, with the Crime Survey estimating about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 Metropolitan Police recording-system change means earlier years over-counted. These are the official baseline figures for trans-hostile incidents in the jurisdiction where the national framework applies directly.

sources.title: Gender Recognition Act 2004
sources.documents: Allows transgender people to change legal gender in the UK, acquire new birth certificate and full recognition of acquired sex; requires evidence to Gender Recognition Panel, 2-year transition, GRC issuance; surgery not required but accepted as evidence; married trans people required to divorce/annul for GRC.
sources.detail: Cited as Gender Recognition Act 2004 (Welsh: Deddf Cydnabod Rhywedd 2004); in force since 4 April 2005

sources.title: Corbett v Corbett (1970)
sources.documents: Court decision that made it legally impossible for transgender people to change sex marker on birth certificate, rendering them unable to marry person of other gender; used as precedent including by US courts.
sources.detail: Cited as 1970 decision of the court case Corbett v Corbett
